profile.headline: Senior Software Engineer at Prepared
profile.summary:
Bill Clinton has said that software development is “a black art, and cannot yet be called an engineering discipline”. Though I disagree with him, it is undeniable that “techno-warlock” is a much more evocative title than “software-engineer”.

    It is this trepidation with which software development is viewed that makes the field so exciting—every line of code I have written, from my current work as a back-end Java developer to the front-end technologies I used during my education and training is written in the preamble of software as a science.  What could possibly be more exciting?

    During my time at The Ohio State University, I specialized in the development of enterprise applications--the functionality, reliability, and scale required interest me at both a conceptual and implementation level.  My education allowed me to experiment with agile project management, Java enterprise servers, full-stack web application development, and even gave me the opportunity to develop an automated regression testbed with Nationwide as my capstone project.

    In my last position at Cerner, I was given the opportunity to work with new Java back-end workflows that interact with Cerner’s EHR, Millenium.  Working on new features for an application that is as old as I am allows me to learn more about the practical considerations of enterprise software development while also giving me space to experiment and learn.  A small point of pride: when I was assigned to my first project, I was warned by another developer that our roadmaps hadn’t allowed me to start with a simple “onboarding” assignment, and that the project to which I had been assigned would actually be more difficult than much of our standard workload.  My second was much the same, except this time I was the sole developer for large chunks of time, as the colleague I was working with was frequently pulled away to address more immediate concerns.  Despite their complexity and my relative inexperience, both projects made their timelines and were included in the first quarterly release since my joining the team.

    Though it is early in my career, I have no doubt that my genuine interest in software and results-driven attitude will see me aggressively producing and refining software solutions for decades to come.
